parallel.problem: Establishing whether past exposure to a price, shock or policy leaves a lasting imprint on consumer or investor behavior (habit or imprinting) rather than simply reflecting current incentives.
parallel.how_studied: Economists use panel data and difference-in-differences designs comparing cohorts that experienced a shock at different times. They include lagged-term regressions and test for persistence after the incentive is removed. Natural experiments, such as a cohort entering the labor market during a recession, provide quasi-random assignment of the initial exposure.

prompt:
Here is a problem from another field that shares the underlying structure of the research question below, with notes on how that field investigates it.

<parallel>
Field: Neuroscience-free cognitive economics (behavioral economics)
Problem: Establishing whether past exposure to a price, shock or policy leaves a lasting imprint on consumer or investor behavior (habit or imprinting) rather than simply reflecting current incentives.
How it is studied: Economists use panel data and difference-in-differences designs comparing cohorts that experienced a shock at different times. They include lagged-term regressions and test for persistence after the incentive is removed. Natural experiments, such as a cohort entering the labor market during a recession, provide quasi-random assignment of the initial exposure.
</parallel>

Each of your ideas must transfer a specific method, measurement logic, or principle from how that field studies its problem, while still being a concrete, scientifically sound way to address the research question.

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: Persistence-after-withdrawal test (washout time course)
ideas.description: Give a transient stimulus (e.g., EGF, TPA, or injury signal), then remove it and track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN) and target gene expression over days of washout. Memory is indicated if accessibility and transcriptional priming persist well beyond AP-1 activity returning to baseline, analogous to testing for effects that persist after the incentive is removed.

ideas.title: Cohort-style timing design with re-stimulation (primed vs naive)
ideas.description: Compare cells exposed at different times or doses (early vs late, single vs repeated) against never-exposed matched controls, then challenge all with the same second stimulus. Use a difference-in-differences model on the response (gene induction, enhancer opening) to estimate the exposure-history effect, controlling for current AP-1 levels, much as cohort comparisons isolate imprinting from current incentives.

ideas.title: Lagged-term regression on single-cell multiome data
ideas.description: In single-cell RNA plus ATAC time series, regress the current state of target loci on both current AP-1 (FOS/JUN) activity and lagged AP-1 activity or past accessibility. A significant lagged coefficient after conditioning on present AP-1 supports memory, while dependence only on current levels supports ongoing incentive-driven regulation.

ideas.title: Acute degradation of AP-1 after the exposure (removing the current incentive)
ideas.description: Use degron-tagged JUN/FOS (dTAG or auxin-inducible) or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS. Degrade AP-1 only after the priming stimulus, then test whether accessibility and enhanced re-induction persist. Compare with degradation before or during priming to separate the role of AP-1 in establishing memory from its role in maintaining it.

ideas.title: Natural-experiment-like quasi-random exposure via heterogeneity or optogenetics
ideas.description: Use optogenetic or chemogenetic control of AP-1 pulses (such as light-inducible FOS/JUN) so that exposure history is assigned randomly across cells or wells, independent of cell state. Measure later chromatin and transcriptional outcomes as a function of pulse number, duration and timing, which gives causal dose-history relationships free of the selection confounds in endogenous exposure.
